function.name: generate_sea_foam
function.description: Simulates the creation of sea foam based on the agitation level of water, amount of organic material, and the presence of salt. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

agitation_level.description: The level of agitation in the water, represented by a scale from 1 (calm) to 10 (very agitated).

organic_material.description: The amount of organic material present in grams per liter. This is a float type value.

salt_presence.description: Indicates whether salt is present (true) or not (false) in the water.

temperature.description: The water temperature in degrees Celsius. If unspecified, defaults to average sea temperature. This is a float type value.

message.content:
The color of the sea isn’t a single, fixed hue—it changes with depth, light, water composition, and the surrounding environment. Here’s a quick rundown:

| Factor | Typical Color | Why it Happens |
|--------|---------------|----------------|
| **Shallow, clear water** | Turquoise / light blue | Light penetrates easily; scattering of shorter wavelengths (blue) dominates, while some green light is also reflected. |
| **Deeper water** | Dark blue | As depth increases, longer wavelengths (red, orange, yellow) are absorbed, leaving mostly blue light. |
| **High phytoplankton concentration** | Greenish‑blue | Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light, reflecting green. |
| **Coastal areas with sediment** | Brownish or muddy | Suspended particles scatter light, giving a brown or gray tint. |
| **Saltwater vs. freshwater** | Slightly different shades | Saltwater tends to be a deeper blue due to higher salinity affecting light absorption. |
| **Sun angle & weather** | Varies from pale blue to deep indigo | Low sun angles (sunrise/sunset) can make the sea appear orange or pink; overcast skies can give a muted gray. |

So, the sea can look anything from a bright turquoise in tropical lagoons to a deep indigo in the open ocean, depending on those variables.
